title: Igor Mezic: Koopman Operator Theory For Dynamical Systems, Control And Data Analytics
speaker: Igor Mezic
one_sentence: This lecture explains Koopman operator theory as a way to represent nonlinear dynamics through a linear operator acting on observables.
core_problem: Nonlinear dynamical systems are difficult to analyze, reduce, and control because the state evolution is nonlinear. Koopman theory changes the viewpoint: instead of evolving states directly, evolve functions of the state. The operator becomes linear, but infinite-dimensional, so the challenge is finding useful observables and spectral decompositions.
first_principles_model: An observable is a function of the system state. The Koopman operator advances observables forward in time by composition with the nonlinear flow. Its eigenfunctions evolve by simple exponential factors, so if useful eigenfunctions are found, nonlinear dynamics can be represented in linear coordinates. Numerical methods such as DMD approximate parts of this operator from data.
key_claims: Koopman theory reformulates dynamical systems in terms of evolving observables.
The Koopman operator is linear even when the original system is nonlinear.
Eigenfunctions give coordinates whose evolution is governed by linear equations.
Koopman decompositions are orthogonal in time rather than necessarily in space.
DMD is one numerical route for approximating Koopman spectra and modes.
POD can confuse dynamics when coherent Koopman structure has not been extracted.

important_terms.meaning: A linear operator that advances observables of a dynamical system by composing them with the system flow.
A function of the state whose evolution can be studied instead of the state itself.
An observable that evolves by multiplication with an exponential factor under the Koopman operator.
Dynamic Mode Decomposition, a data-driven method often used to approximate Koopman modes and eigenvalues.
Persistent dynamical structures whose time behavior can be captured by spectral components.

stanford_connections: This talk links equation discovery, Green's functions, and ROMs through operator-theoretic structure.
It connects to control because linear representations of nonlinear dynamics can simplify feedback and prediction.
It also offers a conceptual alternative to POD-based reduction: choose coordinates by dynamics, not only variance.
practical_caution: Koopman methods depend heavily on the choice or discovery of observables. A finite-dimensional approximation can look linear and still miss important dynamics if the observable space is wrong.
selected_evidence: Koopman operator theory... for dynamical systems control and data analytics.
A reformulation... in terms of evolutionary observables.
The operator is linear.
Eigenfunctions are special functions... governed by linear equations.
DMD is... ways of approximating the Koopman operator.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that nonlinear dynamics may become linear in the right observable space. Koopman theory is a search for that space.

title: Miles Cranmer: The Problem With Deep Learning For Physics And How To Fix It
speaker: Miles Cranmer
one_sentence: This lecture argues that black-box deep learning can create scientific debt in physics and proposes interpretable alternatives such as inductive biases and symbolic regression.
core_problem: Deep learning can solve high-dimensional prediction problems, but if the learned solution is opaque, science may gain performance without understanding. That creates scientific debt: future researchers must explain what the model learned and whether it reflects real mechanism.
first_principles_model: Physics already has an interpretability language: mathematics. Instead of using neural networks only as black-box predictors, one can build physical inductive biases into the architecture, such as Lagrangian neural networks, or distill trained networks into symbolic equations using symbolic regression. The aim is to turn learned patterns into inspectable scientific statements.
key_claims: Using deep learning blindly can postpone the need to understand the physical problem.
Standard interpretation methods from computer vision are not ideal for physics because physics has symbolic mathematical structure.
Inductive bias restricts the space of functions a model can learn toward physically meaningful forms.
Lagrangian neural networks learn a physical quantity inside an existing mechanics framework.
Graph networks are well suited to particle-like physical systems because natural systems are relational rather than only gridded.
Symbolic regression can approximate internal neural-network components with analytic equations.

important_terms.meaning: The accumulated explanatory burden created when a model predicts well without producing scientific understanding.
A prior restriction on what functions a model can learn, often used to encode physical structure.
A search method for analytic equations that fit data or approximate a learned model.
A neural model that learns a Lagrangian or energy-like function and derives dynamics through mechanics equations.
Extracting simpler symbolic formulas from a trained neural network or its learned components.

stanford_connections: This talk is a philosophical and technical counterweight to black-box surrogate modeling throughout the series.
It connects to SINDy, Green's functions, and nonlocal kernels because all emphasize learning interpretable mechanisms.
It also ties back to physics-guided forecasting: inductive bias is not optional decoration, it is what makes models scientifically usable.
practical_caution: A physically inspired neural network can still be degenerate if the prior is too weak or the variables are not identifiable. Interpretability methods should produce testable equations or mechanisms, not just nicer visualizations.
selected_evidence: The problem with deep learning in physics and how to fix it.
We are postponing our need to understand that problem.
Physics has a good symbolic model... math.
An inductive bias is some kind of prior on what possible functions your model can learn.
Symbolic regression... searching for equations.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that scientific ML should repay its explanatory debt. Use neural networks to discover mechanisms, not merely to hide them.

title: Greg Beroza: Towards Complete Machine-Learning-Based Earthquake Monitoring Workflows
speaker: Greg Beroza
one_sentence: This lecture frames earthquake monitoring as an end-to-end scientific workflow where machine learning can improve detection, association, location, and characterization, but only when labels, augmentation, architecture, and catalog validation are treated as part of the system.
core_problem: Earthquake monitoring is not one prediction task. A seismic network produces continuous noisy ground-motion streams, and the operational system must clean traces, detect phases, associate phases into events, locate earthquakes, estimate magnitudes, and maintain catalogs over time. Replacing one step with a neural network helps, but workflow-level errors can still propagate.
first_principles_model: A monitoring workflow converts raw waveforms into a structured earthquake catalog. Each step changes the information representation: signal to phase picks, phase picks to events, events to locations and source properties. Machine learning is useful when it learns these transformations from labeled seismic examples and augmented data, but the final scientific object is the catalog, so the correct unit of evaluation is workflow quality, not just neural-network accuracy on an isolated subtask.
key_claims: Standard earthquake monitoring is a sequence of pre-processing, phase detection, event-phase association, location, and characterization.
Deep learning can replace individual steps and sometimes produces much more complete catalogs than traditional approaches.
Accurate labels, model architecture, and data augmentation are not implementation details; they determine whether the model generalizes to real seismic networks.
A modular strategy is easiest to deploy because it replaces workflow components one by one.
There are advantages to combining multiple monitoring steps in multi-task models because seismic tasks share information.
Better catalogs matter scientifically because small and previously missed earthquakes reveal earthquake occurrence patterns and hazard structure.

important_terms.meaning: A structured record of detected seismic events, including occurrence time, location, magnitude, and related event properties.
Identifying arrival times of seismic wave phases, such as P and S waves, in continuous waveform data.
Grouping phase arrivals across sensors into a coherent earthquake event.
Constructing varied training examples from known seismic signals so a model learns invariances rather than memorizing one network condition.
A modeling approach where related monitoring subtasks are learned jointly instead of as isolated modules.

stanford_connections: This talk is a workflow-level counterpart to earlier PINN and surrogate-model lectures: the learned model must fit inside a scientific pipeline.
It connects to active learning and data engineering because labels and augmentation are central to successful scientific ML.
It also connects to uncertainty and inverse problems: catalog quality determines what downstream geophysical inference can be trusted.
practical_caution: Do not judge a monitoring model only by phase-picking scores. A model can have good local detection metrics and still create bad catalogs if association, location, magnitude estimation, or domain transfer fails.
selected_evidence: Standard earthquake monitoring workflows can be described with... pre-processing, phase detection, event-phase association, location, and characterization.
Machine learning methods, particularly deep neural networks, have been shown capable of replacing these steps.
Generate earthquake catalogs that are far more comprehensive than those developed using standard approaches.
Appropriate architecture, accurate data labels, and data augmentation all play an important role.
The simplest approach... is modular.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that scientific ML for monitoring should be evaluated as a complete measurement system. The output is not a classifier score; it is a catalog that scientists and hazard models will use.

title: Pat Langley: Computational Scientific Discovery
speaker: Pat Langley
organization: Institute for the Study of Learning and Expertise / Stanford Center for Design Research
one_sentence: This lecture presents scientific discovery as heuristic search through spaces of communicable laws and models, guided by data, scientific formalisms, and background knowledge.
core_problem: Mainstream machine learning often optimizes predictive accuracy without producing scientific theories that researchers can communicate, inspect, and reuse. Scientific discovery requires more than fitting curves: it requires searching a structured hypothesis space for laws or models that explain phenomena in a formal language scientists understand.
first_principles_model: A discovery system needs three ingredients: observations to explain, a representational space of possible laws or models, and search heuristics that move through that space. The central constraint is communicability: the result should be a law, equation, qualitative mechanism, or process model that can be stated in an established scientific formalism. Background knowledge narrows the search and makes the candidate models interpretable.
key_claims: Computational discovery can be framed as heuristic search over candidate laws, hypotheses, or models.
Scientific formalisms distinguish discovery systems from generic data mining because the output must be a communicable theory-like object.
Equation discovery searches for numeric laws, but model discovery must also capture qualitative structure and mechanisms.
Qualitative explanatory models can be more important than parameter values because they encode causal or process structure.
Inductive process modeling combines multivariate time series with background knowledge to infer process-based differential equation models.
Domain knowledge is not a nuisance variable; it is what makes search tractable and the result scientifically meaningful.

important_terms.meaning: A guided exploration of a large hypothesis space using rules or scores that prefer promising candidates.
A discovered relationship stated in a compact scientific form, such as an equation or process model, rather than an opaque predictor.
Searching for mathematical equations that fit observed data and express an underlying law.
A model that explains mechanisms or structural relationships even when exact numeric parameters are secondary.
Learning process-based dynamical models from time series using background knowledge and differential equation structure.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects directly to SINDy, symbolic regression, Koopman methods, and Miles Cranmer's discussion of scientific debt.
It offers a philosophical bridge between data-driven modeling and traditional scientific explanation.
It also clarifies why interpretable surrogate models matter: a predictor is not automatically a scientific discovery.
practical_caution: A symbolic expression is not automatically a discovered law. If the hypothesis space, background knowledge, or search heuristic is poorly chosen, the system can produce compact but meaningless equations.
selected_evidence: Discovery involves heuristic search through a space of candidate laws or models.
Those are stated in some established scientific formalism.
That distinguishes work in this area from pretty much everything else in machine learning.
The interesting thing here is not the parameters... the qualitative structure of these laws.
Inductive process modeling... multivariate time series... background knowledge.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that scientific ML should search in the language of science. Data constrains the search, but formalisms and background knowledge make the result communicable.

title: Ashesh Chattopadhyay: Deep Learning Meets Data Assimilation
speaker: Ashesh Chattopadhyay
one_sentence: This lecture explains how deep learning and data assimilation can be combined for chaotic weather and climate forecasting, where sparse noisy observations must be fused with imperfect forecast models.
core_problem: Weather and climate systems are high-dimensional, multiscale, and chaotic. A forecast cannot simply start from perfect truth because observations are noisy, sparse, and unevenly sampled, while numerical or learned forecast models are imperfect. The immediate problem is therefore estimating a usable initial state before forecasting.
first_principles_model: Data assimilation is Bayesian-style state estimation for dynamical systems. A background forecast provides a prior state; observations provide partial noisy evidence; the assimilation algorithm weighs both to produce an analysis state. Deep learning can enter by learning unresolved tendencies, forecast operators, observation-related corrections, or hybrid ensemble Kalman filters, but it must respect dynamical consistency because small state errors can grow rapidly in chaotic systems.
key_claims: Weather and climate forecasting is difficult because the system spans many spatial and temporal scales and is chaotic.
Forecasting requires an initial condition, but observations are sparse and noisy.
Data assimilation fuses background forecasts and observations to estimate the state used to launch prediction.
Deep models can learn effects of unresolved small-scale processes from high-resolution simulations or observations.
Hybrid approaches combine data-driven components with numerical models rather than replacing the whole forecasting pipeline.
Physically consistent architectures and ensemble Kalman filtering are central tools for making learned forecasts operationally useful.

important_terms.meaning: A method for combining model forecasts with noisy observations to estimate the current state of a dynamical system.
The corrected state estimate produced after assimilating observations into a background forecast.
The model-predicted state before observational correction.
A data assimilation method that represents forecast uncertainty with an ensemble and updates it using observations.
A forecasting architecture that combines numerical physics models with learned data-driven components.

stanford_connections: This talk connects to physics-guided learning because model structure matters when small errors amplify through dynamics.
It also links to neural operators and ROMs: learned components must integrate with state estimation, not only free-run forecasting.
The lecture is a practical counterpart to uncertainty lectures because initial-condition uncertainty is a central source of forecast uncertainty.
practical_caution: A neural forecast model that performs well from clean initial states can fail in operational settings if it cannot assimilate noisy sparse observations or if its errors destabilize over time.
selected_evidence: Weather and climate system... is a multi-scale chaotic dynamical system.
Observations... could be noisy, it could be sparse.
Data assimilation... ensure that information from both the background forecast and the noisy observations are properly weighed.
Hybrid sample Kalman filters for weather forecasting.
You can learn the effects... of these small scale processes.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that prediction begins with state estimation. For chaotic physical systems, learning the forecast map and learning how to initialize it are inseparable.

title: Sergei Tretiak: Machine Learning For Materials And Chemical Dynamics
speaker: Sergei Tretiak
one_sentence: This lecture surveys machine learning as a surrogate for materials and chemical dynamics, emphasizing active data generation and the need to overcome locality limits in molecular models.
core_problem: High-fidelity quantum and molecular simulations are expensive, but materials discovery needs many evaluations across structures, configurations, and dynamical regimes. Machine learning can approximate structure-property relationships, yet it fails if training data miss important configurations or if the model's locality assumptions ignore long-range charge, polarization, dispersion, or excited-state effects.
first_principles_model: A molecular ML model maps atomic structure to energies, forces, or properties. Local models gain favorable scaling by decomposing predictions into neighborhoods, but real chemistry can contain nonlocal interactions. Active learning closes the data loop: run the model, detect uncertain configurations, compute new reference data, retrain, and repeat. Nonlocal architectures add interaction layers, self-consistent cycles, or charge-equilibration mechanisms so the surrogate respects broader physical coupling.
key_claims: Machine learning provides surrogate models trained on reference chemical or materials data.
Training data quality is a central determinant of model accuracy because the model can only learn the configurations it sees.
Active learning automatically expands the dataset where model uncertainty is large.
Locality assumptions make atomistic ML scalable but can miss charge transfer, polarization, electrostatics, dispersion, and excited-state effects.
Nonlocal effects can be addressed with interaction layers, self-consistent cycles, and charge-equilibration schemes.
Chemical dynamics requires not just static property prediction but stable behavior across evolving configurations.

important_terms.meaning: A surrogate model that predicts molecular energies and forces from atomic configurations.
A data acquisition loop that adds new reference calculations where the current model is uncertain.
The assumption that an atom's contribution can be predicted mostly from its nearby environment.
A physical effect where distant atoms or global charge structure influence local behavior.
A mechanism that estimates charge redistribution across a molecular system to capture long-range electrostatic effects.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects to data-centric scientific ML: the active learning loop is as important as the network architecture.
It also links to multiscale modeling because local atomic rules must produce reliable material-scale behavior.
It reinforces the series theme that physical inductive bias is often required when extrapolation is dangerous.
practical_caution: A model that is accurate on a benchmark set can still fail in simulation if dynamics carries it into configurations outside the training distribution or into regimes dominated by nonlocal physics.
selected_evidence: Machine learning... provides a surrogate model trained on the dataset of some reference data.
Designing high-quality training data sets is crucial to overall model accuracy.
Active learning strategy... new data are automatically collected for atomic configurations that produce large ML uncertainties.
A major drawback of the current machine learning framework... is locality.
Overcome nonlocality... interaction layers, self-consistent cycles, or charge equilibration schemes.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that molecular ML is a controlled approximation of quantum or atomistic physics. Its reliability depends on where data are gathered and which physical couplings the architecture can represent.

title: Kaushik Bhattacharya: Multi-Scale Modeling And Neural Operators
speaker: Kaushik Bhattacharya
one_sentence: This lecture explains neural operators as function-to-function approximators that can carry fine-scale material physics into efficient coarse-scale multiscale models.
core_problem: Material behavior emerges from interacting physics across electronic, atomistic, defect, domain, and continuum scales. Directly resolving every fine-scale detail inside engineering-scale simulations is often impossible, while crude homogenization can lose the details that control performance.
first_principles_model: Multiscale modeling decomposes the problem into an ordered hierarchy of scales. The coarse scale provides boundary conditions or loading to the fine scale, and the fine scale returns effective responses. A neural operator learns this map between function spaces rather than between finite-dimensional vectors. If trained as a controlled approximation to the fine-scale operator, it can be embedded at the coarse scale with high fidelity and lower cost.
key_claims: Materials involve coupled physics across many length and time scales.
Multiscale modeling uses a divide-and-conquer hierarchy in which coarser scales control and filter finer-scale details.
The practical bottleneck is repeatedly solving expensive fine-scale problems inside coarse-scale computations.
Neural operators approximate maps from one function space to another, which matches the mathematical structure of many physical solution operators.
Operator learning is different from ordinary supervised learning on fixed-size vectors because the input and output are functions.
Neural operators can preserve small-scale detail while making coarse-scale implementation computationally efficient.

important_terms.meaning: A modeling strategy that links physical descriptions across different spatial or temporal scales.
A neural model that learns a map between function spaces, such as from a coefficient field to a solution field.
A set whose elements are functions, making the learning problem infinite-dimensional before discretization.
The larger-scale representation used for engineering simulation or system-level prediction.
The smaller-scale physics, such as atomistic or microstructural behavior, that informs effective large-scale response.

stanford_connections: This lecture is central to the playlist's neural-operator thread and complements talks on FNOs, DeepONets, and ROMs.
It connects operator learning to classical multiscale mechanics rather than treating it as a generic black-box surrogate.
It also links to uncertainty and reliability because coarse-scale predictions inherit approximation errors from learned fine-scale closures.
practical_caution: A neural operator is only useful if it approximates the right operator over the right distribution of functions. Good interpolation on one discretization does not guarantee multiscale validity under new microstructures, loads, or boundary conditions.
selected_evidence: The behavior of materials involve physics at multiple length and time scales.
Multiscale modeling seeks to understand this complexity with a divide and conquer approach.
The maps we are interested in learning is from one function space to another.
We are trying to learn a non-linear operator.
Capture all the details of the small scale but can be directly implemented at the coarse scale.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that operator learning becomes powerful when the learned object matches the physics object: a map between fields, scales, and boundary-conditioned responses.

title: Lexing Ying: Prony's Method, Analytic Continuation, And Quantum Signal Processing
speaker: Lexing Ying
one_sentence: This lecture uses Prony's method as a unifying numerical idea for extracting exponential structure from signals, then applies that idea to noisy analytic continuation and quantum signal processing factorization.
core_problem: Many scientific computing problems ask us to recover hidden spectral or exponential structure from limited samples. This is hard because noise, finite sampling, and ill-conditioning can make frequency identification and analytic continuation unstable. Quantum signal processing adds a related factorization problem where stable phase recovery is essential.
first_principles_model: Prony's method starts from the assumption that a sampled signal is a sum of exponentials. If that model is right, the frequencies and amplitudes are encoded in algebraic relationships among equally spaced samples. The broader lesson is to exploit latent analytic structure: convert a hard inverse problem into identifying the parameters of a structured representation, while respecting noise and conditioning.
key_claims: Prony's method identifies frequencies and amplitudes from equally spaced samples of exponential sums.
The method is old but underappreciated relative to its usefulness in scientific computing.
Noisy analytic continuation can be approached using ideas from Prony-style structured signal recovery.
Quantum signal processing requires stable factorization of phase factors.
The same algebraic insight can connect classical signal processing, complex analytic continuation, and quantum algorithms.
Stability is the central practical issue because the inverse problems are sensitive to noise.

important_terms.meaning: A classical algorithm for recovering frequencies and amplitudes in a signal modeled as a finite sum of exponentials.
Extending a function beyond the region where it is directly known, often an ill-posed problem when data are noisy.
A framework for transforming spectra of quantum operators through sequences of controlled phase factors.
Estimating the exponential or oscillatory components that generate observed samples.
A situation where small data errors can cause large errors in the recovered solution.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects to inverse problems in the series: extracting hidden structure from limited measurements is a recurring theme.
It also complements Koopman and spectral methods because all rely on finding useful frequency or eigen-structure.
It adds a numerical-analysis perspective to the ML-heavy playlist: not every data-driven method is a neural network.
practical_caution: Structured recovery can be powerful, but if the assumed exponential model is wrong or the data are too noisy, Prony-style methods can amplify errors rather than reveal structure.
selected_evidence: Prony's method is a powerful algorithm for identifying frequencies and amplitudes from equally spaced signals.
How many frequencies do you have in the signal... can you figure out what is... the weights.
Applying Prony's method to do noisy analytic continuation.
Stable factorization of the phase factors for quantum signal processing.
The classical solution... goes back more than 200 years.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that good algorithms exploit structure before optimizing. Prony's method works because it turns samples into a parametric spectral model.

title: Ming Zhong: Machine Learning Of Self Organization From Observation
speaker: Ming Zhong
one_sentence: This lecture develops a data-driven framework for learning interaction laws in self-organizing collective systems directly from observed trajectories.
core_problem: Self-organization appears in systems such as flocking, crowds, crystals, superconductivity, and social behavior. The macroscopic pattern may be visible, but the microscopic interaction rule among agents is unknown. The challenge is to infer physically meaningful dynamical laws from observations rather than only forecast trajectories.
first_principles_model: A collective system can be modeled as interacting agents whose velocities or accelerations depend on pairwise distances, states, and agent types through interaction kernels. Given trajectory data from multiple initial conditions, the learning problem is to estimate those kernels so the resulting dynamical system reproduces observed behavior and predicts new collective motion. Theory studies convergence as data from initial conditions increases.
key_claims: Self-organization can be studied through observed trajectories of interacting agents.
The goal is to derive interpretable dynamical systems and interaction rules, not only black-box predictions.
Learning interaction kernels can validate and improve existing models of collective behavior.
Convergence analysis depends on data from multiple initial conditions and on how trajectory data are discretized.
The framework extends from homogeneous agents to heterogeneous systems such as predator-prey interactions.
Steady-state observations can also contain information about interaction kernels, though the inverse problem requires regularization.

important_terms.meaning: Collective behavior where large-scale order emerges from local interactions among components or agents.
A function describing how one agent influences another as a function of distance, state, or type.
Agents governed by the same interaction laws.
Agents of different types with different interaction rules, such as predators and prey.
Time-indexed observations of agent states used to infer the governing interaction laws.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects to equation discovery and symbolic modeling because it learns governing laws from data.
It also links to nonlocal kernels and graph-based physics: collective behavior depends on relational interactions.
It complements forecasting talks by emphasizing interpretable dynamics over pure trajectory extrapolation.
practical_caution: Inferring interaction laws from observation is an inverse problem. Good trajectory fit does not guarantee a unique or physically correct kernel, especially with limited initial conditions or steady-state-only data.
selected_evidence: Self-organization... can be found in studying crystal formation, superconductivity, social behaviors.
Can we actually derive from observation data... the interaction rules between all the agents.
Develop a learning framework to derive physically meaningful dynamical systems.
Analyze the convergence... from various different initial conditions.
Handle a system of heterogeneous agents.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that collective patterns are compressed evidence about interaction laws. Scientific ML should recover the laws, not just replay the pattern.

title: Alice Cicirello: Interpretable, Explainable And Non-Intrusive Uncertainty Propagation
speaker: Alice Cicirello
one_sentence: This lecture explains how machine-learning-based optimization can propagate interval uncertainty through expensive black-box engineering models while preserving interpretability, explainability, and non-intrusiveness.
core_problem: Engineering decisions depend on whether a system satisfies performance bounds under uncertainty, but high-fidelity physics models can be expensive to evaluate. Standard uncertainty propagation may require too many model runs or intrusive changes to the solver, making it impractical for expensive engineering simulations.
first_principles_model: Uncertainty propagation asks how uncertain inputs map through a computational model into uncertain performance outputs. A non-intrusive method treats the simulator as a black box and chooses a small number of evaluations. Machine-learning optimization, especially Bayesian optimization-style sampling, can search for output bounds while explanations and interpretable surrogate structure help humans understand why those bounds arise.
key_claims: Uncertainty quantification supports decisions by estimating how input uncertainty affects system performance.
For expensive-to-evaluate models, the main bottleneck is selecting as few physics-model runs as possible.
Non-intrusive methods avoid modifying the simulator or simplifying the underlying physics.
Interpretability asks whether a human can understand how a prediction was made.
Explainability asks whether results are presented in a form that humans can use.
Machine-learning optimization can target performance bounds rather than densely sampling the full input space.

important_terms.meaning: Computing how uncertainty in model inputs affects uncertainty in model outputs or performance metrics.
A method that uses an existing simulator as a black box without altering its equations or implementation.
Uncertainty represented as ranges of possible values rather than full probability distributions.
A sample-efficient optimization method that uses a probabilistic surrogate to choose informative evaluations.
An upper or lower limit on a quantity of interest under uncertain inputs.

stanford_connections: This talk connects to the series' uncertainty theme and gives a decision-oriented version of surrogate modeling.
It also links to active learning because both select evaluations strategically under expensive data generation.
It complements interpretability talks by defining explanation as a requirement for engineering uncertainty decisions.
practical_caution: A non-intrusive UQ method can miss true extremes if the sampling strategy or surrogate is overconfident. Performance bounds should be treated as certified only when the search and validation assumptions justify them.
selected_evidence: Uncertainty models are used in conjunction with a computational model to compute the effects of uncertainties on a system performance.
Interpretable: a human can understand how a prediction was made.
Explainable: the results are presented in a format that is understandable by humans.
Non-intrusive: no modifications of the computational model are carried out.
Select the minimum number of physics based models to run in order to get performance bounds.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that UQ is a decision problem under computational scarcity. The method must choose simulations efficiently and explain the resulting bounds clearly.

title: Yannis Kevrekidis: No Equations, No Variables, No Parameters, No Space And No Time
speaker: Yannis Kevrekidis
one_sentence: This lecture argues that modern data-driven modeling can sometimes bypass explicit equations, variables, parameters, space, and time by discovering useful coarse observables and computational representations directly from observations.
core_problem: Classical modeling moves from observations to variables, equations, parameters, and analysis. Complex systems often resist this route because the right macroscopic variables are unknown, the microscopic simulator may be available without closed equations, and the effective geometry or time scale may be hidden inside high-dimensional data.
first_principles_model: The first-principles move is to separate the scientific task from the traditional symbolic container. If the goal is prediction, continuation, bifurcation analysis, or control, one can sometimes build the required computational operators directly from data or short bursts of simulation. Manifold learning, diffusion maps, autoencoders, recurrent nets, neural ODEs, and operator learning can identify low-dimensional coordinates, coarse observables, or evolution rules without first writing a closed-form macroscopic equation.
key_claims: Many modern neural architectures have older roots in nonlinear dynamical-system identification.
Equation-free modeling keeps the analysis goal but replaces explicit macroscopic equations with computational experiments on data or microscopic simulators.
The right variables may be learned from data rather than chosen by intuition alone.
Manifold learning can reveal low-dimensional curved structure inside high-dimensional observations.
Diffusion maps are one way to learn coordinates on data manifolds that serve as macro observables.
The provocative phrase no equations, variables, parameters, space, or time points to learning the representation needed for the task rather than assuming it in advance.

important_terms.meaning: A computational framework that performs macroscopic analysis using data or microscopic simulators without closed-form macroscopic equations.
A reduced variable that summarizes the large-scale state of a complex system.
Methods that discover low-dimensional geometric structure inside high-dimensional data.
A manifold-learning method that uses diffusion geometry on data to construct useful low-dimensional coordinates.
A computational operator that advances coarse variables by lifting them to microscopic states, simulating briefly, and restricting back.

stanford_connections: This talk links directly to Petros Koumoutsakos' effective dynamics lecture and later data-driven dynamics talks.
It also connects to ROMs and neural operators because all search for lower-dimensional or operator-level descriptions.
It reframes scientific ML as representation discovery: first learn what variables or coordinates make the problem solvable.
practical_caution: Learning coordinates from data is powerful only if the data cover the relevant manifold. A beautiful low-dimensional embedding can fail under new regimes, rare transitions, or unobserved parameters.
selected_evidence: No equations no variables no space no time.
Obtaining predictive dynamical equations from data lies at the heart of science and engineering modeling.
Operate directly on observations -data-.
Machine learning on the data to find out what the right macro observables are.
Diffusion Maps... learn low dimensional curved manifolds passing through the data.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that equations are one representation of dynamics, not the only one. The deeper goal is to find the coordinates and operators that make prediction and analysis possible.

title: Weinan E: Machine Learning And Multi-Scale Modeling
speaker: Weinan E
one_sentence: This lecture explains how machine learning helps multiscale modeling by representing complex functions and closures that classical hand-built models struggle to express.
core_problem: Multiscale modeling aims to connect quantum, atomistic, coarse-grained, continuum, and turbulence-level descriptions into practical simulations of properties of interest. The idea is compelling, but hard problems remain because effective models and closure relations can be too complex to derive or parameterize manually.
first_principles_model: Each scale has a model that is useful in its own regime. The multiscale task is to pass information between scales: fine models supply effective laws, closures, potentials, or constitutive relations for coarser models. Machine learning expands the representational toolkit for these interscale maps, allowing learned potentials, coarse-grained dynamics, non-Newtonian constitutive models, and reduced PDE models.
key_claims: Multiscale modeling is an attempt to unify physical models across scales for accurate simulation protocols.
Its practical success has been limited by difficulty representing complex functions and complex models.
Machine learning offers flexible representations for closures and effective models.
Applications include molecular dynamics, coarse-grained molecular dynamics, non-Newtonian fluid dynamics, and PDE model reduction.
The hierarchy of physical models spans quantum mechanics, density functional theory, molecular dynamics, coarse-grained models, continuum mechanics, and turbulence models.
The central promise is not replacing physics, but learning the pieces that connect physical descriptions across scales.

important_terms.meaning: A framework for linking models defined at different physical scales to predict macroscopic quantities of interest.
An approximate relation that represents unresolved fine-scale effects inside a coarser model.
A molecular simulation approach that groups fine degrees of freedom into larger effective units.
A fluid whose stress-strain relationship cannot be described by a constant viscosity Newtonian law.
A model at one scale that summarizes relevant effects of more detailed lower-scale physics.

stanford_connections: This lecture pairs naturally with Kaushik Bhattacharya's neural-operator view of multiscale mechanics.
It also connects to materials ML because learned potentials are one concrete multiscale bridge.
It reinforces a recurring theme: ML is most useful when it fills a representational gap in a physics pipeline.
practical_caution: A learned closure can be accurate inside its training regime and still break conservation, stability, or transfer across scale if it is not embedded consistently in the larger simulator.
selected_evidence: Multi-scale modeling... aims at unifying the different physical models at different scales.
Practical success on really challenging problems has been limited.
Limited ability to represent complex models and complex functions.
Machine learning has emerged as a promising tool for overcoming the difficulty.

takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that multiscale ML is about learning interfaces between physical descriptions. The model is valuable when it lets a trusted simulation reason across scales.

title: Daniel Floryan: Charting Dynamics From Data
speaker: Daniel Floryan
one_sentence: This lecture uses the geometry of manifolds and atlases of charts to learn minimal dynamical models directly from time-series data.
core_problem: Many systems are high-dimensional, nonlinear, and difficult to derive first-principles equations for, yet their trajectories often live on lower-dimensional structures. A single global coordinate system may distort that structure or fail entirely, so the modeling problem is to find local coordinates and dynamics that together cover the state space.
first_principles_model: A manifold can be represented by an atlas: overlapping local coordinate charts with maps between local coordinates and the ambient state. From time-series data, one can cluster trajectories into patches, learn coordinates on each patch, learn local dynamics, and stitch the patches into a global dynamical description. The result is a minimal model in the intrinsic dimension of the system rather than the dimension of the measured state.
key_claims: Data-driven model discovery is motivated by unknown governing equations and high-dimensional known equations.
Natural systems often evolve on low-dimensional manifolds inside high-dimensional state spaces.
An atlas of charts provides local coordinate systems for covering a manifold.
Time-series data can be clustered into overlapping patches that become coordinate domains.
Learning local charts can produce dynamical models in the lowest useful dimension.
Local charting can separate state-space geometry from coordinate artifacts and improve prediction or control.

important_terms.meaning: A space that may be globally curved but looks locally like a low-dimensional Euclidean space.
A collection of overlapping charts that together describe a manifold.
A local coordinate representation of one patch of a manifold.
The true low-dimensional degrees of freedom needed to describe the system's state.
Sequential observations of a system used to infer its geometry and dynamics.

stanford_connections: This lecture complements Kevrekidis' representation-discovery theme with a concrete geometric construction.
It also connects to ROMs because both seek low-dimensional dynamical descriptions.
It is a bridge between manifold learning, nonlinear dynamics, and control-oriented model discovery.
practical_caution: Local charts require good coverage and overlap. If the data miss parts of the manifold or transitions between patches, the learned atlas can produce discontinuous or misleading dynamics.
selected_evidence: Learn minimal dynamical models directly from time series data.
Natural systems tend to live on small or low dimensional manifolds.
A manifold is... an atlas of charts.
Time series data... lie on or near a manifold.
Cluster the data into overlapping patches.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that dimension reduction is not just compression. For dynamical systems, the learned coordinates must support a valid evolution law.

title: Petros Koumoutsakos: Artificial Intelligence And Scientific Computing For Fluid Mechanics
speaker: Petros Koumoutsakos
one_sentence: This lecture argues for forming careful alloys of AI and scientific computing for complex flows, using learned effective dynamics and multi-agent reinforcement learning while distinguishing real progress from hype.
core_problem: Fluid mechanics combines nonlinear dynamics, multiscale structure, turbulence, flow-structure interaction, and control. AI methods are widely promoted as replacements for simulation, but black-box learning alone is unreliable for complex flows. The problem is how to combine data, numerical solvers, physical insight, and learning algorithms into systems that predict and control flows better than either component alone.
first_principles_model: Scientific computing provides discretized physical laws, numerical solvers, and stability constraints. AI provides flexible approximation, representation learning, and control policies. An alloy is a hybrid in which each component does what it is structurally good at: simulators generate or constrain dynamics, learned models approximate effective low-dimensional behavior, and reinforcement learning explores control strategies under physical simulation feedback.
key_claims: AI has benefited from massive hardware and data growth, but fluid-mechanics claims require careful separation of promise from hype.
Complex flow prediction and control should use fusions of AI and simulations rather than naive replacement.
Learning effective dynamics is one alloy: microscopic or high-fidelity simulations inform a reduced dynamical description.
The equation-free framework is an important ancestor of learned effective dynamics.
Multi-agent reinforcement learning can be fused with scientific computing for flow-structure interaction and control.
Successes and failures both matter because they reveal when physical structure is necessary.

important_terms.meaning: A hybrid computational system that combines scientific computing, models, numerics, and machine learning.
A reduced dynamical description that captures the behavior of a complex system at the scale of interest.
Coupled dynamics between a fluid and moving or deforming solid bodies.
A learning setup where multiple agents learn policies through interaction with an environment and each other.
Numerical methods and computational algorithms for solving mathematical models of physical systems.

stanford_connections: This lecture directly extends Kevrekidis' equation-free and effective-dynamics ideas into fluid mechanics.

It also links to RL-based scientific control, where simulation becomes the training environment.
practical_caution: For fluids, a learned model that looks impressive on one rollout can fail under distribution shift, unstable long-time integration, or control feedback. Hybridization must include numerical and physical checks.
selected_evidence: There is an ever-increasing amount of hype... regarding the capabilities of learning algorithms.
Forming alloys of AI and simulations for the prediction and control of complex flow systems.
Models and numerics and... machine learning tools... I call this computing alloys.
Learning the effective dynamics of complex systems.
Equation free framework... simulations in the microscales.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that AI for fluids should be engineered as a hybrid scientific-computing system. The right question is not AI or solvers, but which alloy is stable, accurate, and controllable.

title: Benjamin Peherstorfer: Neural Galerkin Schemes With Active Learning
speaker: Benjamin Peherstorfer
one_sentence: This lecture presents Neural Galerkin schemes that solve high-dimensional evolution equations by fitting neural-network states over time and actively selecting training samples guided by PDE residuals.
core_problem: High-dimensional time-dependent PDEs are difficult because uniform sampling of the time-space domain can be wasteful, while neural networks need informative data to realize their approximation power. Static training sets may miss moving localized structures such as waves, fronts, or coherent features.
first_principles_model: Galerkin methods approximate a PDE solution inside a chosen trial space by enforcing residual conditions. Neural Galerkin replaces the classical trial basis with a neural-network representation whose parameters evolve sequentially in time. Instead of drawing all training points blindly, the method uses residual information to actively collect samples where the current approximation needs them most.
key_claims: Estimating population loss is hard in science and engineering when informative samples are scarce.
Neural Galerkin schemes fit network parameters by minimizing PDE residuals sequentially over time.
Residual-based sampling provides a self-informed active-learning mechanism.
Active data collection is key to making neural approximation capabilities practical in high dimensions.
The approach is especially relevant for evolution equations with moving coherent features.
The method reframes training data generation as part of the numerical solver rather than a preprocessing step.

important_terms.meaning: A numerical method that approximates a solution in a trial space and enforces residual orthogonality or minimization.
A Galerkin-style PDE solver whose trial space is parameterized by a neural network.

A differential equation describing how a system changes over time.

practical_caution: Residual minimization can be misleading if the sampling distribution misses important regions or if the residual is small while the solution error is large. Active learning reduces this risk but does not remove the need for validation.

Few informative training samples are available.
Neural Galerkin schemes... generate training data samples with active learning.

takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that neural PDE solvers should adapt their samples to the dynamics. The training set is part of the numerical method.

title: Ishan Khurjekar: Uncertainty-Aware Guided Wave Structural Health Monitoring
speaker: Ishan Khurjekar
one_sentence: This lecture explains how ensemble learning and probabilistic methods can make guided-wave structural health monitoring more robust to uncertainty from temperature, loading, and model mismatch.
core_problem: Guided-wave SHM systems detect and localize damage by comparing acoustic wave signals across sensor arrays. Real structures experience temperature, loading, and environmental variations that change wave propagation, so damage-like signal changes may arise even when the structure is healthy. Vanilla neural networks can be overconfident under these shifts.
first_principles_model: A guided-wave monitoring system sends waves through a structure and records received signals. Damage changes those signals, but nuisance variables such as temperature also change them. Uncertainty-aware learning treats detection and localization as probabilistic inference: ensembles, variational autoencoders, adversarial perturbations, and anomaly detection estimate both predictions and confidence under variation.
key_claims: Structural health monitoring is important for buildings, bridges, aircraft, oil rigs, and other infrastructure.
Guided waves are useful for damage detection and localization because sensor arrays can transmit and receive acoustic waves.
Temperature and loading variations create uncertainty by changing wave propagation even without damage.
Deep learning methods need uncertainty awareness because ordinary networks can be brittle or overconfident.
Ensembles of variational autoencoders can improve robustness to temperature variation.
Adversarial training on simulated perturbations can improve robustness to wave-number uncertainty.

takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that monitoring is not just classification. It is inference under environmental variation, and uncertainty is part of the output.

title: Tailin Wu: Learning To Accelerate Large-Scale Physical Simulations
speaker: Tailin Wu
one_sentence: This lecture presents learned simulators for large-scale fluid and plasma systems, using graph networks, U-Nets, and multi-step objectives to improve long-term rollout and multiscale behavior.
core_problem: Large-scale fluid and plasma simulations can involve millions of cells and expensive long-time evolution. Deep surrogate models promise speedups, but they must handle heterogeneous geometry, local and global dynamics, multiscale coupling, and error accumulation over rollouts.
first_principles_model: A physical simulator updates a field state over time. A learned simulator approximates that update map. For subsurface flow, local water-oil dynamics can be represented by graph neural networks over mesh cells, while pressure has more global structure suited to U-Net-like field models. Training on multi-step losses exposes the model to its own rollout errors, improving long-term stability compared with one-step imitation.

Deep surrogate modeling can complement or accelerate simulations but faces long-term evolution and multiscale dynamics challenges.

Graph neural networks are useful for irregular or mesh-based local interactions.
Multi-step training objectives improve long-term rollout accuracy compared with one-step losses.

title: Molei Tao: Trustworthy Learning Of Mechanical Systems And Stiefel Optimization
speaker: Molei Tao
one_sentence: This lecture shows how hard-wiring geometric structure such as symplecticity into learned mechanical dynamics improves long-time prediction, and connects dynamics ideas to optimization on the Stiefel manifold.
core_problem: Mechanical systems preserve geometric structures such as energy behavior, momentum, and symplecticity. Standard neural predictors can fit short trajectories while violating these structures, causing long-time drift. Optimization on constrained manifolds such as the Stiefel manifold has a related problem: algorithms should respect the geometry of the space they move on.
first_principles_model: A mechanical system is not just a sequence of states; it is a flow with preserved geometric structure. Symplectic learning builds this preservation into the model so the learned time evolution remains faithful over long horizons. For Stiefel optimization, the variable lies on the manifold of orthonormal frames, so gradient dynamics and momentum acceleration must be designed on the manifold rather than in unconstrained Euclidean space.
key_claims: Physics hard-wired into deep learning models can improve trustworthy prediction of mechanical dynamics.
Mechanical systems preserve structures such as energy, momentum, and symplecticity.
Symplecticity is an underlying geometric property of Hamiltonian dynamics.
Hard-wiring symplectic structure can provably improve long-time prediction accuracy.
The interaction between dynamics and machine learning also informs optimization algorithms.
Momentum-accelerated gradient descent can be constructed on Riemannian manifolds, with the Stiefel manifold as a key example.

important_terms.meaning: A geometric structure preserved by Hamiltonian mechanical dynamics.

Forecasting a dynamical system over many time steps where small structural errors can accumulate.

Optimization methods designed for variables constrained to curved manifolds.

title: Dirk Hartmann: Machine Learning And Physics-Based Simulations For Industrial Digital Twins
speaker: Dirk Hartmann
one_sentence: This lecture frames industrial digital twins as hybrid systems where machine learning and physics-based simulation must be tightly integrated to achieve usable accuracy, speed, and automation.
core_problem: Industrial assets, products, systems, and infrastructure need digital models that are accurate enough for decisions and fast enough for design, engineering, and operations. Pure high-fidelity simulation is often too slow and expert-intensive, while pure ML can be unreliable outside the data regime. Scaling digital twins also runs into the cost of manual expert modeling effort.
first_principles_model: A digital twin is a computational representation tied to a real asset or process. In industry, it must answer operational questions under constraints: speed, accuracy, maintainability, and deployment cost. Physics-based models provide structure and extrapolation discipline; machine learning supplies fast surrogates, calibration, automation, and data adaptation. The useful object is the hybrid workflow, not either component alone.

Research needs should be judged from the full industrial lifecycle, not only academic benchmark performance.

title: Ricardo Vinuesa: Modeling And Controlling Turbulent Flows Through Deep Learning
speaker: Ricardo Vinuesa

CNNs can map wall measurements to off-wall velocity fields; transfer learning can reuse structure across Reynolds numbers; autoencoders can build nonlinear ROMs; GANs can reconstruct high-resolution flow from sparse or low-resolution data; reinforcement learning can search for control policies in simulation.

title: Santi Adavani: Industrial Grade Scientific Machine Learning
speaker: Santi Adavani

SciML must therefore be evaluated along three axes: whether the problem formulation is unambiguous, whether the method scales to industrial sizes and compute environments, and whether it can be deployed, monitored, and maintained.

title: Ben Erichson: Continuous Networks For Sequential Predictions
speaker: Ben Erichson

title: Benjamin Sanderse: Structure-Preserving Learning Of Embedded Discrete Closure Models
speaker: Benjamin Sanderse

one_sentence: This lecture explains how neural closure models for PDEs should be learned while embedded inside discretized solvers, with structure preservation such as kinetic-energy conservation to avoid instability.
core_problem: Closure models represent the effect of unresolved small scales on resolved large scales in LES, ROMs, and other reduced descriptions. Adding structure-preserving forms, such as kinetic energy conservation, gives nonlinear stability bounds.

title: Eric de Sturler: Cheap And Robust Adaptive Reduced Order Models For Nonlinear Inversion And Design
speaker: Eric de Sturler
one_sentence: This lecture explains how randomization and adaptive reduced-order models can reduce the cost of nonlinear inverse and PDE-constrained optimization problems while monitoring surrogate accuracy.
core_problem: Nonlinear inverse problems and design optimization often require repeated large linear, nonlinear, and adjoint solves. Parametric ROMs can reduce cost, but building and evaluating them can still be expensive, and they often lack cheap error bounds during optimization.
first_principles_model: Optimization with a surrogate is safe only if the optimizer knows when the surrogate is reliable. Randomization can cheaply construct reduced bases or estimate errors and objective improvement gaps. Adaptive ROMs update the reduced model when monitoring indicates it is no longer accurate enough, and trust-region logic limits steps according to surrogate reliability.
key_claims: Nonlinear inverse and PDE-constrained optimization problems require many repeated solves.
Newton-type methods also require adjoint or transpose-system solves.
Parametric model reduction and surrogate models can substantially reduce computation.
Online computation of reduced models can itself be expensive for these problems.
Parametric ROMs often lack cheap error bounds.
Randomization can help compute reduced models cheaply and monitor accuracy or objective improvement for trust-region methods.

important_terms.meaning: A problem of estimating unknown parameters or structures from observations when the forward map is nonlinear.
Optimization where the variables must satisfy a PDE model.
A reduced model designed to approximate a family of full models across parameter values.
Using randomized numerical methods to reduce cost, estimate error, or sample informative subspaces.
An optimization method that restricts steps to regions where the model is believed to be reliable.

stanford_connections: This lecture connects ROMs to inverse design and optimization rather than only forward simulation.
It also links to uncertainty and error monitoring because surrogate use requires reliability estimates.
It complements industrial SciML by asking how reduced models can be made cheap and robust enough for repeated design loops.
practical_caution: A reduced model can accelerate optimization while steering it in the wrong direction if its error is not monitored. Trust-region or randomized error checks are part of the algorithm, not optional diagnostics.
selected_evidence: Nonlinear inverse problems and other PDE-constrained optimization problems... require the repeated solution of many discretized large linear systems.
For Newton-type methods we also need solutions for the adjoint problem.
Parametric model reduction or other surrogate models as well as by randomization.
Reduced order models do not come with (cheap) error bounds.
Monitor the difference between the reduced model and full model objective function improvement.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that optimization needs trustworthy cheap models, not just cheap models. The surrogate must know when it is safe to guide the next step.

title: Zorin Mitran: Data-Driven Information Geometry For Stochastic Model Reduction
speaker: Zorin Mitran
organization: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
one_sentence: This lecture extends reduced-order modeling from flat Euclidean subspaces to curved statistical manifolds, using data-driven information geometry for stochastic systems.
core_problem: Standard ROMs often project data onto linear subspaces using Euclidean least squares. For stochastic phenomena, the objects of interest are probability distributions, and their natural geometry may be curved rather than flat. In non-equilibrated systems, a clean parametric distribution family may not even be known.
first_principles_model: Information geometry treats families of probability distributions as manifolds with metrics and geodesics. Instead of projecting vectors onto a linear subspace, stochastic model reduction projects or transports distributions along curved statistical manifolds. When no parametric family is given, local normal distributions can be constructed from data using SVD, and their envelope forms a data-driven statistical manifold.
key_claims: Traditional ROMs project onto subspaces and minimize Euclidean distance in flat linear spaces.
Stochastic phenomena can be modeled on manifolds of probability distributions.
Information geometry studies statistical manifolds of parametrized probability distributions.
For non-equilibrated systems, an explicit parametrized distribution may be unavailable.
A data-driven statistical manifold can be built from envelopes of local normal distributions obtained from SVD of data.
Reduced models are obtained by geodesic transport, where geodesics are curved rather than straight Euclidean lines.

important_terms.meaning: The study of probability distributions as geometric objects on statistical manifolds.
A manifold whose points represent probability distributions.
The shortest or natural path between points on a curved manifold, generalizing straight lines.
A local Gaussian approximation built around data neighborhoods.
Reducing the complexity of models whose states or outputs are probabilistic.

stanford_connections: This lecture broadens the ROM theme from deterministic state reduction to probabilistic distribution reduction.
It connects to uncertainty quantification because model states are treated as distributions rather than point estimates.
It also links to manifold-learning talks: the reduced object may live on a curved learned geometry.
practical_caution: A Euclidean projection can distort probabilistic structure. For stochastic systems, the choice of geometry affects the reduced model, so the manifold construction must match the distributional behavior in the data.
selected_evidence: Reduced-order models are often obtained by projection onto a subspace.
Extension... from flat spaces to curvilinear manifolds of probability distributions.
Information geometry is the study of statistical manifolds.
Envelope of local normal distributions obtained from the singular value decomposition of data.
Reduced-order models are obtained by geodesic transport.
takeaway: The first-principles lesson is that stochastic reduction is geometry-sensitive. If the objects are distributions, the reduced space should respect distribution geometry.
